blocks.instruction: Choose TWO letters, A–E, for each question.

people.name: Orla Fenwick
people.role: psychologist who studied delayed train passengers' estimates of waiting time

people.name: Bilal Haddad
people.role: operations manager of a passport office who redesigned its queuing system

people.name: Yuna Sorensen
people.role: consumer researcher who criticises perception-based queue management

paragraphs.text: Few experiences are as universal, or as quietly frustrating, as standing in a queue. The line might lead to a supermarket checkout, a hospital reception desk or a theme-park ride. Either way, most people have felt a ten-minute wait drag on as though it were half an hour, and an equally long one pass almost unnoticed. Psychologists who study queues explain this by separating two kinds of time: the duration a clock would record and the duration a person actually experiences. For the organisations that make customers wait, the second figure frequently matters more than the first. Satisfaction depends less on how long people stand in line than on how long they believe they have stood there.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: One of the most reliable findings is that empty time feels longer than occupied time. When there is nothing to do, attention turns to the passing of time itself, and every minute becomes noticeable. This is why so many waiting areas offer something to look at or handle. Hotels and office buildings often hang mirrors beside lifts. People waiting for the doors to open can check their appearance or discreetly observe others, and complaints about slow lifts tend to fall as a result. A related effect concerns the moment at which a service seems to begin. People who are still waiting to be acknowledged feel more impatient than those who sense that the process is under way. This is why a restaurant that hands diners a menu as soon as they sit down makes them feel that their meal has already started, even if the kitchen has not yet received the order.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Uncertainty is another powerful influence. A wait of unknown length feels longer than one whose end is in sight, and a delay that nobody explains feels longer than one with an obvious cause. Both conditions produce anxiety, and anxiety appears to stretch time: the worried mind keeps checking whether anything has changed. In one study, the psychologist Orla Fenwick asked passengers on a train held outside a station to estimate how long they had been stationary. In some carriages the driver had made a brief announcement explaining the hold-up, and passengers there guessed, on average, several minutes less than those in carriages where the speakers had failed. Yet both groups had waited exactly the same time. Fenwick cautions that her sample came from a single railway line, but the result fits a wider pattern: information, even unwelcome information, makes waiting easier to bear.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Perhaps the strongest feelings in any queue concern fairness. Most cultures expect queues to follow the principle of first come, first served, and seeing someone who arrived later reach the front first can cause more irritation than the wait itself. Multiple parallel lines, common in older supermarkets, make such injustices highly visible, since one line inevitably moves faster than its neighbours. A single line that feeds several counters removes the problem, because every customer is served strictly in order of arrival. People tend to rate it as fairer even when the average wait is no shorter. The arrangement has a weakness, however. A single line serving many counters can grow very long, and newcomers who see it may decide not to join at all. For this reason some firms break it up with ropes and bends, so that no one can see its full length at once.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: These principles can be combined, as a project led by Bilal Haddad, the operations manager of a busy passport office, illustrates. Haddad began by asking his team to spend a month observing the public hall. They found that complaints rose sharply whenever visitors could see no sign of progress. Their first change was to replace the five separate lines in front of the counters with one single line that served all of them. Next, they installed screens displaying the expected wait. The estimates were kept deliberately pessimistic, so that most visitors would be called sooner than predicted and feel pleasantly surprised. Visitors were then given a numbered ticket, which allowed them to wait in a nearby café rather than stand in the hall. Finally, each person was asked to fill in a short form while waiting, which kept them occupied and also reduced the time needed at the counter. After six months, the average wait had barely changed, yet complaints had fallen by half.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes this kind of management. Yuna Sorensen, a consumer researcher, argues that techniques designed to shorten perceived time can become a substitute for shortening real time. An organisation that installs entertaining screens, she points out, may feel less pressure to employ the extra staff who would actually reduce delays. She is also uneasy about deliberately pessimistic estimates, which may persuade some customers to give up and leave before they have joined the queue at all. Her criticisms do not mean that the psychology of waiting should be ignored. Rather, they suggest that the most successful approach combines genuine improvements in speed with honest information and thoughtful design, so that customers wait less and also feel that they have waited less.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
Why the Wait Feels Long

A. Few experiences are as universal, or as quietly frustrating, as standing in a queue. The line might lead to a supermarket checkout, a hospital reception desk or a theme-park ride. Either way, most people have felt a ten-minute wait drag on as though it were half an hour, and an equally long one pass almost unnoticed. Psychologists who study queues explain this by separating two kinds of time: the duration a clock would record and the duration a person actually experiences. For the organisations that make customers wait, the second figure frequently matters more than the first. Satisfaction depends less on how long people stand in line than on how long they believe they have stood there.

B. One of the most reliable findings is that empty time feels longer than occupied time. When there is nothing to do, attention turns to the passing of time itself, and every minute becomes noticeable. This is why so many waiting areas offer something to look at or handle. Hotels and office buildings often hang mirrors beside lifts. People waiting for the doors to open can check their appearance or discreetly observe others, and complaints about slow lifts tend to fall as a result. A related effect concerns the moment at which a service seems to begin. People who are still waiting to be acknowledged feel more impatient than those who sense that the process is under way. This is why a restaurant that hands diners a menu as soon as they sit down makes them feel that their meal has already started, even if the kitchen has not yet received the order.

C. Uncertainty is another powerful influence. A wait of unknown length feels longer than one whose end is in sight, and a delay that nobody explains feels longer than one with an obvious cause. Both conditions produce anxiety, and anxiety appears to stretch time: the worried mind keeps checking whether anything has changed. In one study, the psychologist Orla Fenwick asked passengers on a train held outside a station to estimate how long they had been stationary. In some carriages the driver had made a brief announcement explaining the hold-up, and passengers there guessed, on average, several minutes less than those in carriages where the speakers had failed. Yet both groups had waited exactly the same time. Fenwick cautions that her sample came from a single railway line, but the result fits a wider pattern: information, even unwelcome information, makes waiting easier to bear.

D. Perhaps the strongest feelings in any queue concern fairness. Most cultures expect queues to follow the principle of first come, first served, and seeing someone who arrived later reach the front first can cause more irritation than the wait itself. Multiple parallel lines, common in older supermarkets, make such injustices highly visible, since one line inevitably moves faster than its neighbours. A single line that feeds several counters removes the problem, because every customer is served strictly in order of arrival. People tend to rate it as fairer even when the average wait is no shorter. The arrangement has a weakness, however. A single line serving many counters can grow very long, and newcomers who see it may decide not to join at all. For this reason some firms break it up with ropes and bends, so that no one can see its full length at once.

E. These principles can be combined, as a project led by Bilal Haddad, the operations manager of a busy passport office, illustrates. Haddad began by asking his team to spend a month observing the public hall. They found that complaints rose sharply whenever visitors could see no sign of progress. Their first change was to replace the five separate lines in front of the counters with one single line that served all of them. Next, they installed screens displaying the expected wait. The estimates were kept deliberately pessimistic, so that most visitors would be called sooner than predicted and feel pleasantly surprised. Visitors were then given a numbered ticket, which allowed them to wait in a nearby café rather than stand in the hall. Finally, each person was asked to fill in a short form while waiting, which kept them occupied and also reduced the time needed at the counter. After six months, the average wait had barely changed, yet complaints had fallen by half.

An organisation that installs entertaining screens, she points out, may feel less pressure to employ the extra staff who would actually reduce delays. She is also uneasy about deliberately pessimistic estimates, which may persuade some customers to give up and leave before they have joined the queue at all. Her criticisms do not mean that the psychology of waiting should be ignored. Rather, they suggest that the most successful approach combines genuine improvements in speed with honest information and thoughtful design, so that customers wait less and also feel that they have waited less.
